title: The Million Dollar Homepage
hook: A student sold a web page one pixel at a time and made a million dollars.
peek: In 2005 a 21-year-old British student named Alex Tew set up a web page with a million pixels and sold them for a dollar each to pay for university. Within five months every pixel was gone.
lede: In August 2005 Alex Tew, a 21-year-old from Wiltshire about to start a business degree at the University of Nottingham, wanted a way to pay for it. He made a single web page, 1,000 by 1,000 pixels, and offered the space to advertisers at one dollar a pixel. Each buyer got a small image and a link. The idea caught on fast.

bullets.text: Pixels were sold in blocks of 100, so the smallest ad cost 100 dollars. Buyers ranged from small websites to bigger firms, and the page became a dense, colourful patchwork of tiny logos.

bullets.opening: Press coverage and word of mouth
bullets.text: After a few early sales to friends and family, news stories picked it up. Each article sent more visitors, and more visitors persuaded more advertisers. The page drew huge traffic for months.
Tew auctioned the last 1,000 pixels on eBay in January 2006, and they fetched 38,100 dollars. In total the page brought in just over a million dollars before costs.
The page is still online, frozen as it was in 2006, but many of the sites it links to have since vanished. It has become a snapshot of the early web and of how quickly links stop working.
